sentence: 'If the auditors had read the memo, they would have raised precisely the objection we see in their report. We still need to check whether they received it.'
setupText: Choose what the conditional itself establishes about whether the memo was read.
taskText: 'If the auditors had read the memo, they would have raised precisely the objection we see in their report. We still need to check whether they received it.'
text: Choose what the conditional itself establishes about whether the memo was read. 'If the auditors had read the memo, they would have raised precisely the objection we see in their report. We still need to check whether they received it.'
options: It establishes that the auditors did not read the memo.
It establishes that the auditors received but ignored the memo.
It establishes that reading the memo was the only possible source of the objection.
It leaves reading unresolved while assessing its expected consequence.
answer: It leaves reading unresolved while assessing its expected consequence.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-941:Limits of counterfactual falsity inferences
explanation: The speaker considers what reading would lead to without resolving whether reading occurred.

rationales.It establishes that the auditors did not: A past-perfect conditional often suggests a contrary-to-fact premise, but this context explicitly leaves reading unresolved.
rationales.It establishes that the auditors receive: Receipt and neglect are not established; the next sentence calls for checking receipt.
rationales.It leaves reading unresolved while asses: The speaker considers what reading would lead to without resolving whether reading occurred.
rationales.It establishes that reading the memo was: An expected consequence does not establish that its proposed cause was the only possible cause.

sentence: 'The permit remains valid unless the holder fails to renew the insurance.'
setupText: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the exception and its negation exactly.
taskText: 'The permit remains valid unless the holder fails to renew the insurance.'
text: Choose the paraphrase that preserves the exception and its negation exactly. 'The permit remains valid unless the holder fails to renew the insurance.'
options: If the holder fails to renew the insurance, the permit remains valid.
If the holder does not fail to renew the insurance, the permit remains valid.
The permit remains valid only if the holder fails to renew the insurance.
Unless the holder renews the insurance, the permit remains valid.
answer: If the holder does not fail to renew the insurance, the permit remains valid.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-942:Negation scope inside an unless exception
explanation: Unless negates the whole exception, including fails: in the absence of failure to renew, validity continues.

rationales.If the holder fails to renew the insuran: This turns the stated exception into a condition guaranteeing continued validity.
rationales.If the holder does not fail to renew the: Unless negates the whole exception, including fails: in the absence of failure to renew, validity continues.
rationales.The permit remains valid only if the hol: Only if makes failure necessary for validity, reversing the original protection.
rationales.Unless the holder renews the insurance,: This makes renewal, rather than failure to renew, the exception.

sentence: The editor wants to state two commitments: without approval there is no release, and approval guarantees release.
setupText: Choose the rule that makes approval both necessary and sufficient for release.
taskText: The editor wants to state two commitments: without approval there is no release, and approval guarantees release.
text: Choose the rule that makes approval both necessary and sufficient for release. The editor wants to state two commitments: without approval there is no release, and approval guarantees release.
options: The report will be released if approval is granted.
The report will be released if and only if approval is granted.
The report will be released only if approval is granted.
The report may be released if approval is granted.
answer: The report will be released if and only if approval is granted.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-943:Biconditional commitment versus one-way conditions
explanation: If and only if states both directions: approval is required and is enough for release.

rationales.The report will be released if approval: If grants the approval-to-release direction but does not rule out release by another route.
rationales.The report will be released only if appr: Only if makes approval necessary but does not promise release when approval is granted.
rationales.The report may be released if approval i: May gives a possibility even after approval, not the requested guarantee.
rationales.The report will be released if and only: If and only if states both directions: approval is required and is enough for release.

sentence: 'Would you endorse the plan?' 'Not if it involves compulsory overtime.'
setupText: Choose the interpretation supported by the reply.
taskText: 'Would you endorse the plan?' 'Not if it involves compulsory overtime.'
text: Choose the interpretation supported by the reply. 'Would you endorse the plan?' 'Not if it involves compulsory overtime.'
options: Removing compulsory overtime guarantees the speaker's endorsement.
The speaker asserts that the plan already involves compulsory overtime.
Compulsory overtime would rule out the speaker's endorsement.
The speaker endorses compulsory overtime but questions the rest of the plan.
answer: Compulsory overtime would rule out the speaker's endorsement.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-944:Conditional negation in an elliptical reply
explanation: Not if supplies a condition under which the answer to endorsing is no.

rationales.Compulsory overtime would rule out the s: Not if supplies a condition under which the answer to endorsing is no.
rationales.Removing compulsory overtime guarantees: Ruling out one condition for refusal does not guarantee endorsement for other reasons.
rationales.The speaker asserts that the plan alread: The reply identifies a possible disqualifier without asserting that it is present.
rationales.The speaker endorses compulsory overtime: The specified objection is to compulsory overtime; no endorsement of it is expressed.

sentence: 'The revisions have made the policy harsher.' 'If anything, they've made it more flexible.'
setupText: Choose the function of 'if anything' in this response.
taskText: 'The revisions have made the policy harsher.' 'If anything, they've made it more flexible.'
text: Choose the function of 'if anything' in this response. 'The revisions have made the policy harsher.' 'If anything, they've made it more flexible.'
options: The speaker remains neutral between the two assessments.
The speaker cautiously proposes the opposite assessment.
Flexibility depends on whether any revision exists.
The speaker agrees that harshness and flexibility increased equally.
answer: The speaker cautiously proposes the opposite assessment.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-945:Corrective idiom if anything
explanation: 'If anything' introduces a tentative correction in the opposite direction: more flexible rather than harsher.

rationales.The speaker remains neutral between the: The hedge is cautious, but the speaker does favor the opposite assessment, more flexible.
rationales.Flexibility depends on whether any revis: This is an idiomatic corrective phrase, not an ordinary event condition.
rationales.The speaker cautiously proposes the oppo: 'If anything' introduces a tentative correction in the opposite direction: more flexible rather than harsher.
rationales.The speaker agrees that harshness and fl: The reply challenges the first assessment; it does not endorse both equally.

sentence: The writer means 'The study is useful, but I am not claiming it is indispensable.' The draft says, 'The study is useful, if not indispensable.'
setupText: Choose the edit that unambiguously expresses the intended modest claim.
taskText: The writer means 'The study is useful, but I am not claiming it is indispensable.' The draft says, 'The study is useful, if not indispensable.'
text: Choose the edit that unambiguously expresses the intended modest claim. The writer means 'The study is useful, but I am not claiming it is indispensable.' The draft says, 'The study is useful, if not indispensable.'
options: The study is useful, though not necessarily indispensable.
The study is indispensable, if not useful.
If the study is indispensable, it is useful.
The study is useful only if it is indispensable.
answer: The study is useful, though not necessarily indispensable.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-946:Disambiguating scalar if not
explanation: Though not necessarily explicitly withholds the stronger claim and avoids the draft's possible 'perhaps even' reading.

rationales.The study is indispensable, if not usefu: This promotes indispensable to the asserted description, stronger than intended.
rationales.The study is useful, though not necessar: Though not necessarily explicitly withholds the stronger claim and avoids the draft's possible 'perhaps even' reading.
rationales.If the study is indispensable, it is use: This makes usefulness conditional on indispensability rather than asserting usefulness directly.
rationales.The study is useful only if it is indisp: Only if makes indispensability necessary for usefulness, which the intended modest claim does not require.

sentence: The curator trusted an unreliable account and now wishes she had checked it.
setupText: Choose the sentence that expresses regret about the past, without making a rule about evidence.
taskText: The curator trusted an unreliable account and now wishes she had checked it.
text: Choose the sentence that expresses regret about the past, without making a rule about evidence. The curator trusted an unreliable account and now wishes she had checked it.
options: Only if I had checked the account would I have trusted it.
If I check the account, I can decide whether to trust it.
If only I had checked the account before trusting it.
If only I check the account, the decision is mine.
answer: If only I had checked the account before trusting it.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-947:If only versus only if and subject-focus only
explanation: 'If only' plus past perfect expresses a wish that a completed past choice had been different.

rationales.Only if I had checked the account would: Only if states a necessary condition for trusting; it does not express the curator's regret.
rationales.If I check the account, I can decide whe: This sets up a current or future checking condition rather than wishing the past were different.
rationales.If only I check the account, the decisio: Here 'only' restricts the subject 'I'; it does not form the intended past regret.
rationales.If only I had checked the account before: 'If only' plus past perfect expresses a wish that a completed past choice had been different.

sentence: 'The files will be opened to researchers unless both the donor objects and the committee upholds the objection.'
setupText: Choose the statement licensed by the rule without deciding whether the exception occurs.
taskText: 'The files will be opened to researchers unless both the donor objects and the committee upholds the objection.'
text: Choose the statement licensed by the rule without deciding whether the exception occurs. 'The files will be opened to researchers unless both the donor objects and the committee upholds the objection.'
options: If either the donor objects or the committee objects, the files must stay closed.
The donor's objection alone prevents the files from being opened.
The committee has already upheld the donor's objection.
If the donor objects but the committee rejects the objection, the files will be opened.
answer: If the donor objects but the committee rejects the objection, the files will be opened.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-948:Unless with a conjunctive exception
explanation: The exception requires both stated events; rejection by the committee means that combined exception is absent.

rationales.If the donor objects but the committee r: The exception requires both stated events; rejection by the committee means that combined exception is absent.
rationales.If either the donor objects or the commi: This substitutes either/or for the rule's both/and and changes the committee's action.
rationales.The donor's objection alone prevents the: The donor's objection alone does not meet the two-part exception.
rationales.The committee has already upheld the don: The rule sets a future condition; it reports no completed committee decision.

sentence: A: 'Even if the witness is mistaken, the timestamps establish the sequence.' B: 'Even though the witness is mistaken, the timestamps establish the sequence.'
setupText: Choose the distinction accurately made by the two versions.
taskText: A: 'Even if the witness is mistaken, the timestamps establish the sequence.' B: 'Even though the witness is mistaken, the timestamps establish the sequence.'
text: Choose the distinction accurately made by the two versions. A: 'Even if the witness is mistaken, the timestamps establish the sequence.' B: 'Even though the witness is mistaken, the timestamps establish the sequence.'
options: A leaves the mistake open; B presents it as a conceded fact.
A asserts the mistake more firmly than B does.
B makes the timestamps depend on the witness being correct.
A and B both deny that the timestamps establish the sequence.
answer: A leaves the mistake open; B presents it as a conceded fact.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-949:Factual commitment in concessive alternatives
explanation: The difference is factual commitment to the concession, while the claim about the timestamps remains.

rationales.A asserts the mistake more firmly than B: Even if does not itself assert the mistake; even though normally concedes it as fact.
rationales.B makes the timestamps depend on the wit: B says the timestamps establish the sequence despite the mistake, not because the witness is correct.
rationales.A leaves the mistake open; B presents it: The difference is factual commitment to the concession, while the claim about the timestamps remains.
rationales.A and B both deny that the timestamps es: Both versions assert the evidential role of the timestamps.

sentence: 'If either the identity check or the payment check is incomplete, access must be withheld.'
setupText: Choose the equivalent condition for withholding access.
taskText: 'If either the identity check or the payment check is incomplete, access must be withheld.'
text: Choose the equivalent condition for withholding access. 'If either the identity check or the payment check is incomplete, access must be withheld.'
options: Access must be withheld only when both checks are incomplete.
If the two checks are not both complete, access must be withheld.
If either check is complete, access must be withheld.
If neither check is incomplete, access must be withheld.
answer: If the two checks are not both complete, access must be withheld.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-950:Negation across either/or conditions
explanation: Not both complete covers either incomplete check or both incomplete checks, preserving the original trigger.

rationales.Access must be withheld only when both c: The original triggers withholding when even one check is incomplete, not only when both are.
rationales.If the two checks are not both complete,: Not both complete covers either incomplete check or both incomplete checks, preserving the original trigger.
rationales.If either check is complete, access must: A complete check is not itself the reason for withholding; the other check's status matters.
rationales.If neither check is incomplete, access m: 'Neither incomplete' means 'both complete', reversing the triggering condition.

sentence: The main report will be published regardless. The appendix will be included only with the interviewees' consent.
setupText: Choose the rewrite that makes only the appendix, not the main report, depend on consent.
taskText: The main report will be published regardless. The appendix will be included only with the interviewees' consent.
text: Choose the rewrite that makes only the appendix, not the main report, depend on consent. The main report will be published regardless. The appendix will be included only with the interviewees' consent.
options: If the interviewees consent, we will publish both the report and the appendix; otherwise neither will appear.
We will publish the report only if the interviewees consent, and we may include the appendix.
If we publish the report, the interviewees will consent to the appendix.
We will publish the report; we will include the appendix only if the interviewees consent.
answer: We will publish the report; we will include the appendix only if the interviewees consent.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-951:Scope of a condition over coordinated actions
explanation: Separate clauses keep the report unconditional and attach the consent requirement specifically to the appendix.

rationales.If the interviewees consent, we will pub: This makes the main report conditional too, contrary to its unconditional publication.
rationales.We will publish the report only if the i: This attaches consent to the report and leaves the appendix without the intended restriction.
rationales.If we publish the report, the interviewe: This reverses the dependency and predicts consent from publication.
rationales.We will publish the report; we will incl: Separate clauses keep the report unconditional and attach the consent requirement specifically to the appendix.

sentence: There is no independent audit. With one, we could place greater confidence in the figures now.
setupText: Choose the formal sentence preserving a present absence and a current hypothetical result.
taskText: There is no independent audit. With one, we could place greater confidence in the figures now.
text: Choose the formal sentence preserving a present absence and a current hypothetical result. There is no independent audit. With one, we could place greater confidence in the figures now.
options: Were there an independent audit, we could place greater confidence in the figures now.
Had there been an independent audit last year, we could have trusted last year's figures.
Should an independent audit arrive next year, we will trust the figures then.
Since there is an independent audit, we can place greater confidence in the figures now.
answer: Were there an independent audit, we could place greater confidence in the figures now.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-952:Existential inversion with controlled time and factual status
explanation: Were there imagines reversing the present absence; could preserves a current hypothetical possibility.

rationales.Were there an independent audit, we coul: Were there imagines reversing the present absence; could preserves a current hypothetical possibility.
rationales.Had there been an independent audit last: This moves both the condition and the trust judgment to last year.
rationales.Should an independent audit arrive next: This changes the present alternative into a future contingency and future judgment.
rationales.Since there is an independent audit, we: Since asserts the audit's existence, contrary to the stated absence.

sentence: The overnight log shows no monitoring took place, and we are still reconstructing the failure. If someone ___ the system during the outage, we would now know where it began.
setupText: Choose the completion that links an ongoing unreal past activity with the situation now.
taskText: The overnight log shows no monitoring took place, and we are still reconstructing the failure. If someone ___ the system during the outage, we would now know where it began.
text: Choose the completion that links an ongoing unreal past activity with the situation now. The overnight log shows no monitoring took place, and we are still reconstructing the failure. If someone ___ the system during the outage, we would now know where it began.
options: had been monitoring
is monitoring
will have monitored
were to start monitoring
answer: had been monitoring
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-953:Past-perfect progressive condition with present knowledge result
explanation: Had been monitoring imagines sustained observation during the past outage; its information would be available now.

rationales.is monitoring: 'Is monitoring' describes activity now, not an unreal activity during the completed outage.
rationales.will have monitored: Will have monitored places completion in the future and cannot supply the missing observation from the outage.
rationales.had been monitoring: Had been monitoring imagines sustained observation during the past outage; its information would be available now.
rationales.were to start monitoring: This imagines a prospective start rather than sustained observation during the completed outage.

sentence: 'You should attend the briefing, if only to learn who is responsible for the handover.'
setupText: Choose the meaning of 'if only to' in this recommendation.
taskText: 'You should attend the briefing, if only to learn who is responsible for the handover.'
text: Choose the meaning of 'if only to' in this recommendation. 'You should attend the briefing, if only to learn who is responsible for the handover.'
options: Attendance is advisable only if finding out who is responsible is your purpose.
Finding out who is responsible is the one benefit the speaker allows that attendance could offer.
Finding out who is responsible is reason enough to attend, whatever other benefits there may be.
Whether attendance is advisable remains uncertain until you know who is responsible.
answer: Finding out who is responsible is reason enough to attend, whatever other benefits there may be.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-954:Minimal justification versus necessary purpose, exclusive benefit and uncertainty
explanation: 'If only to' presents a modest benefit as sufficient reason to attend without excluding additional benefits.

rationales.Attendance is advisable only if finding: This turns the highlighted reason into a necessary condition on your purpose; 'if only to' offers it as sufficient support for attending.
rationales.Finding out who is responsible is reason: 'If only to' presents a modest benefit as sufficient reason to attend without excluding additional benefits.
rationales.Finding out who is responsible is the on: 'Only' highlights a minimum justification here; it does not restrict the briefing to a single possible benefit.
rationales.Whether attendance is advisable remains: The recommendation is already made. The phrase supplies a reason to attend, not an unresolved condition delaying the advice.

sentence: After residents were given two minutes to respond, a councillor says, 'If that counts as consultation, the word has lost its meaning.'
setupText: Choose the speaker's rhetorical purpose.
taskText: After residents were given two minutes to respond, a councillor says, 'If that counts as consultation, the word has lost its meaning.'
text: Choose the speaker's rhetorical purpose. After residents were given two minutes to respond, a councillor says, 'If that counts as consultation, the word has lost its meaning.'
options: To announce a neutral definition of consultation.
To confirm that residents approved the proposal.
To challenge whether the process deserves the label consultation.
To suggest the process merely needs a different name.
answer: To challenge whether the process deserves the label consultation.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-955:Rhetorical conditional challenging a category
explanation: The conditional tests a disputed classification and uses an unacceptable consequence to challenge it.

rationales.To announce a neutral definition of cons: The context and exaggerated consequence express criticism, not a neutral definition.
rationales.To confirm that residents approved the p: Nothing in the remark reports approval by residents.
rationales.To suggest the process merely needs a di: The councillor criticizes the process's failure to involve residents; changing its name alone does not address that criticism.
rationales.To challenge whether the process deserve: The conditional tests a disputed classification and uses an unacceptable consequence to challenge it.

sentence: 'If you complete the pilot, we will reimburse the travel costs.' Nothing is said about other reimbursement arrangements.
setupText: Choose the inference justified by the promise alone, without adding an unstated restriction.
taskText: 'If you complete the pilot, we will reimburse the travel costs.' Nothing is said about other reimbursement arrangements.
text: Choose the inference justified by the promise alone, without adding an unstated restriction. 'If you complete the pilot, we will reimburse the travel costs.' Nothing is said about other reimbursement arrangements.
options: Anyone who does not complete the pilot is ineligible for any reimbursement.
Anyone reimbursed must have completed the pilot.
The pilot is complete because reimbursement has been promised.
Completing the pilot is sufficient to trigger the promised reimbursement.
answer: Completing the pilot is sufficient to trigger the promised reimbursement.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-956:Resisting conditional perfection in a promise
explanation: The promise guarantees reimbursement when the stated condition is met.

rationales.Completing the pilot is sufficient to tr: The promise guarantees reimbursement when the stated condition is met.
rationales.Anyone who does not complete the pilot i: The sentence does not say only if; other reimbursement routes remain unstated.
rationales.Anyone reimbursed must have completed th: This reverses the implication and wrongly makes completion necessary for any reimbursement.
rationales.The pilot is complete because reimbursem: A conditional promise does not assert that its condition has already been fulfilled.

sentence: 'The director offered an apology, if apology is the right word for such a defensive statement.'
setupText: Choose what the if-clause qualifies.
taskText: 'The director offered an apology, if apology is the right word for such a defensive statement.'
text: Choose what the if-clause qualifies. 'The director offered an apology, if apology is the right word for such a defensive statement.'
options: Whether the director made any statement at all.
Whether the statement will persuade the people who received it.
Whether apology is an appropriate description of the statement.
Whether the statement will be issued in the future.
answer: Whether apology is an appropriate description of the statement.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-957:Metalinguistic conditional qualification
explanation: The conditional questions the wording used to classify an already mentioned statement.

rationales.Whether the director made any statement: The main clause presents a statement as having been offered; the reservation concerns its label.
rationales.Whether the statement will persuade the: The reservation concerns the category apology, not a prediction of its persuasive effect.
rationales.Whether apology is an appropriate descri: The conditional questions the wording used to classify an already mentioned statement.
rationales.Whether the statement will be issued in: Offered locates the statement in the past; the qualification does not make it a future event.

sentence: 'If you WILL keep changing the requirements after approval, you can't expect us to hold the original deadline.'
setupText: Choose the reading of stressed 'WILL' supported by the speaker's irritation.
taskText: 'If you WILL keep changing the requirements after approval, you can't expect us to hold the original deadline.'
text: Choose the reading of stressed 'WILL' supported by the speaker's irritation. 'If you WILL keep changing the requirements after approval, you can't expect us to hold the original deadline.'
options: A neutral prediction that requirements may change once.
A statement that a regulation requires the listener to make changes.
An admission that the speaker already changed the deadline.
An objection to the listener's persistent insistence on making changes.
answer: An objection to the listener's persistent insistence on making changes.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-958:Stressed volitional will in a reproach
explanation: The stressed modal criticizes insistent repeated behavior and links it to an unreasonable expectation.

rationales.A neutral prediction that requirements m: Stress on 'WILL' and 'keep changing' convey persistence and irritation, not a neutral one-off forecast.
rationales.An objection to the listener's persisten: The stressed modal criticizes insistent repeated behavior and links it to an unreasonable expectation.
rationales.A statement that a regulation requires t: The utterance attributes the behavior to the listener's insistence, not an external rule.
rationales.An admission that the speaker already ch: The speaker rejects an expectation; no actual deadline change is reported.

sentence: The backup was not verified before Monday's test. With prior verification, the team would not have had to pause that test halfway through.
setupText: Choose the condition that preserves an already completed safeguard before a particular past test.
taskText: The backup was not verified before Monday's test. With prior verification, the team would not have had to pause that test halfway through.
text: Choose the condition that preserves an already completed safeguard before a particular past test. The backup was not verified before Monday's test. With prior verification, the team would not have had to pause that test halfway through.
options: If the backup is being verified now, the team would not have had to pause Monday's test.
If the backup had been verified beforehand, the team would not have had to pause Monday's test.
If the backup were to be verified next week, the team would not have had to pause Monday's test.
If the backup had been being verified during the pause, the team would not have had to pause Monday's test.
answer: If the backup had been verified beforehand, the team would not have had to pause Monday's test.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-959:Prior completion versus ongoing or later counterfactual conditions
explanation: The past-perfect passive with beforehand places the unreal completed verification before the past need to pause.

rationales.If the backup is being verified now, the: Verification now cannot serve as the completed safeguard before Monday's past test.
rationales.If the backup were to be verified next w: Verification next week occurs too late to change the specified need during Monday's test.
rationales.If the backup had been being verified du: An ongoing check during the pause does not establish completed verification before the test began.
rationales.If the backup had been verified beforeha: The past-perfect passive with beforehand places the unreal completed verification before the past need to pause.

sentence: 'If these records are authentic, the shipment left before the inspection.'
setupText: Choose the rewrite preserving a condition on the speaker's evidence, not a cause of the reported event.
taskText: 'If these records are authentic, the shipment left before the inspection.'
text: Choose the rewrite preserving a condition on the speaker's evidence, not a cause of the reported event. 'If these records are authentic, the shipment left before the inspection.'
options: The records' authenticity supports concluding that departure preceded inspection.
Authenticating the records caused the shipment to leave before inspection.
The shipment could leave early only after the records were authenticated.
Because the shipment left early, the records must be authentic.
answer: The records' authenticity supports concluding that departure preceded inspection.
focusKey: coverage-conditionals-c2-960:Evidence condition versus causal or procedural condition
explanation: The if-clause states when the records justify the conclusion about an already completed event.

rationales.The records' authenticity supports concl: The if-clause states when the records justify the conclusion about an already completed event.
rationales.Authenticating the records caused the sh: The sentence does not make present authentication a cause of a past departure.
rationales.The shipment could leave early only afte: This changes an evidential condition into a procedural requirement for departure.
rationales.Because the shipment left early, the rec: This reverses the reasoning and treats one reported event as proof of authenticity.
